articles.title: Brazil’s real sinks after Lula’s re-election victory
articles.summary: Investors react to Lula’s victory with a sharp decline in the real and concern over increased spending and fiscal challenges.
articles.body:
Brazil’s real dropped against the United States dollar on the heels of Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s unexpected re-election after right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, led in the first round of voting earlier this month.

Brazil’s currency dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading. Bovespa stock index futures tumbled nearly 15 percent on Monday.

“I’m not surprised the real is sinking sharply; traders are covering their bets that assume a Bolsonaro victory and tighter fiscal policy,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.

Brazil’s stock exchange halted trading for 30 minutes. The Bovespa index fell 10 percent from its previous close, triggering a circuit-breaker safety mechanism and reversing a rally earlier this month amid expectations of a shift to the right after Bolsonaro won the first round.

Ziemba says Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede the election has driven some financial uncertainty.

“The market pressure is also amplified by the objections raised by Bolsonaro, but the scale of the victory suggests that the result will stand,” she said.

Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy under Bolsonaro would allow borrowing costs to decline.

“They [investors] assume more domestic spending and higher rates in Brazil. However, the real is still likely to be supported by strong commodity revenues,” Ziemba noted.

Stocks closed on Friday almost 7 percent above their level before the first round, while the Brazilian real was nearly 5 percent stronger against the US dollar.

Interest rate futures are up 3.1 percent, rising sharply after President Lula’s win. Interest rate futures had previously reflected a tighter fiscal policy amid expectations that Bolsonaro would oust the incumbent and that he would allow borrowing costs to decline.

Lula faces an increase in Brazil’s debt and will be challenged with protecting both social programmes and investment, with investors looking for signs of whether his gradual fiscal approach can bring borrowing costs down.

Lula’s team aims to produce a budget surplus of about 1.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030. That would leave money to cover part of the interest bill, reducing the need for fresh borrowing. But public debt already exceeds 82 percent of GDP, while pensions and other legally required spending limit where savings can come from.

“Lula’s policies have talked about spending cuts, but he has not gone into the details of how that is going to look,” said Divya Singaravelu, head of research at Meridian 1305 Capital.

Attention will now turn to Lula’s choice of finance minister and what it signals about his fiscal approach.

One company that's going to benefit big time from Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) growth over the coming years: SpaceX ( SPCX ).

For SpaceX, it's another feather in its hat for its AI data center compute business, which is now shown to be durable. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen discussed growth in the company's SI business ventures during its Q3 earnings call .

"There are many customers asking for compute, and we're actively building the supply to meet both internal and external demand. We expect to have additional new customers in future deals and will continuously evaluate the highest-margin usage for our compute assets across both new and existing cloud service agreements, including serving inference for our own SI products. What we're seeing in the market is extraordinary."

Johnsen added that at current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year, with pricing "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the 30 to $50 per watt range." Johnsen had previously said he expects SpaceX to hit an annual recurring revenue figure (ARR) of $100 billion by year-end.

Not to be outdone, CEO Elon Musk said he sees SpaceX's ARR hitting between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027. articles.title: 12 new terms Anthropic says you must understand before investing in the company
articles.summary: There is corporate jargon, and then there is the Anthropic IPO prospectus.
articles.body:
There is run-of-the-mill corporate jargon, and then there is the next level of corporate jargon found in the early pages of the newly filed Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO prospectus.

If you are eyeing an investment in the company on IPO day — or ever — you will have to understand the corporate jargon supplied by Anthropic. It's very likely to be tossed around on earnings calls, 10-Qs, 10-Ks, and investment banking conferences.

You'll probably hear similar jargon when rival OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) goes public sometime in 2027.

Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending

5 unexpected risk factors Anthropic is worried about

Anthropic is losing $80 billion on paper — and just made money where it counts

Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion compared to $1.1 billion a year ago, the prospectus shows. However, the filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss and a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.

Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation at close to $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.

Anthropic listed a total of 39 terms in the early pages of its prospectus. Some like "AI" are straightforward, but many others are not. Yahoo Finance selected the ones that may be foreign to you — save this list for easy use come Anthropic IPO day.

Agent loop: "Refers to the iterative cycle in which an AI agent receives a task, takes an action, such as planning a project, running code, or calling a tool, observes the result, and decides its next step, with this cycle repeating until the task is complete. The agent loop is the core execution pattern underlying agentic AI behavior."

Applied AI: "Refers to a discipline and organizational function focused on embedding AI capabilities directly into production business environments to address specific customer requirements. Applied AI teams, which include forward-deployed engineers, work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to a customer's own systems and processes."

Compute multipliers: "Refer to algorithmic and methodological improvements in training and inference that increase the effective output of a given amount of compute."

Constitutional AI: "Refers to an approach to training AI models using a set of written principles, which we refer to as Claude's constitution, currently organized around four priorities: being broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with our guidelines, and genuinely helpful. Under Constitutional AI, our models evaluate, critique, and revise their own responses against these principles, enabling us to define and control model behavior through auditable principles, rather than relying solely on fixed rule-based instructions or human reviewers."

articles.title: DoorDash in exclusive talks to acquire Instacart
articles.summary: A combination would create a delivery giant.
articles.body:
DoorDash is in exclusive talks to acquire Instacart, according to people familiar with the matter.

A deal is far from certain and the talks could fall apart, the people cautioned. It could not be determined what price was under discussion or how a deal would be structured.

Instacart declined to comment. DoorDash did not immediately return a request for comment. Instacart's sale process was first reported by the Information. The Information also reported that Uber was interested in a deal for Instacart, but Bloomberg later reported that that interest had cooled.

A combination would create a home-delivery giant, fusing Instacart's grocery-store centric platform with DoorDash's restaurant-focused one. DoorDash previously bid for Instacart in 2021, but at a significantly higher valuation. Those talks collapsed over price and worries about antitrust pushback, neither of which hold true today. Instacart has a valuation of roughly $12 billion, but at a conservative premium would likely fetch around $15 billion. DoorDash has a market capitalization of roughly $75 billion.

The grocery and home delivery space faces stiff competition chiefly from Amazon and Walmart, which has pressured conventional grocers for years.

The companies would likely not face antitrust issues as well: the Trump administration has taken a light-touch approach to other mergers, including a mammoth combination between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount. But dealmakers expect that window to close, or at least shift, if Democrats succeed at the ballot box next month: senior Democrats have already said they will look to probe antitrust approvals and closed deals.

articles.title: FICO stock falls 14% after Pulte pledges 'more action' on credit score competition

articles.body:
Fair Isaac Corporation ( FICO ) stock dropped more than 13% on Monday after Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte said the agency was focusing on mortgage credit score competition.

"We are taking more action this week to ensure competition is real and not fake, or manipulated," Pulte posted on X , referring to a news story about FICO's decision to hold the price for preferred mortgage lenders to use its score at $10.

Investors and analysts viewed FICO's decision to hold prices flat after several years of hikes as a defensive move to help the company maintain its market share in the face of new competition . A stock slide that started earlier Monday accelerated after Pulte's post.

For decades, FICO was the primary credit score provider for the mortgage industry, and in recent years, the company dramatically hiked prices for its credit scores. As recently as 2022, a single FICO score cost less than $1, but by last year, the company was charging $10 for a two-score bundle.

This year, in a bid to stoke competition, the FHFA began allowing mortgage lenders to use VantageScore , which is provided by credit bureaus Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, for conventional mortgages bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. A single VantageScore costs around $0.99.

Pulte has made credit score pricing a focus for his agency and has been a vocal critic of FICO's pricing practices. In addition to allowing VantageScore for conventional mortgages, he simplified the credit score pricing process for Fannie Mae- and Freddie Mac-eligible loans.

articles.title: I asked Claude to explain Anthropic’s IPO
articles.summary: Before the substance, a disclosure that matters for your story: I’m Claude, made by Anthropic, the company in this filing.
articles.body: What does Anthropic’s chatbot, Claude, think about the big initial public offering? I asked. (Responses in bold.) Before the substance, a disclosure that matters for your story: I’m Claude, made by Anthropic, the company in this filing. Nice work, Claude! I laughed out loud at this. Looks like Anthropic’s AI chatbot demonstrates at least a basic understanding of journalistic ethics. Check every figure against the filing itself, and cite the SEC document rather than me. An important caveat. Don’t worry, Claude, I’ll be doing that. OK, onto the summary of Anthropic’s filing, which Claude boiled down to these five sentences. 1) Anthropic’s revenue went from about $4.6 billion in all of 2025 to $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026. Anthropic is growing at an astounding pace, and Claude’s synopsis actually undersells that fact a bit. When comparing Anthropic’s first-half sales this year to its first-half sales last year (a more apples-to-apples comparison), the company’s revenue grew 1,300%. Of course, no one expects that pace to keep up as the AI business matures, and Anthropic uses the word “slow” 36 times in its prospectus. 2) It is still spending enormous sums on computing power, and it has committed to hundreds of billions of dollars more. Right. This is one of the two big concerns about investing in Anthropic: The amount of money it has committed to spend on computing power (and cloud services — you left that part out, Claude) is worrisome, making Anthropic (and any AI hyperscaler) a particularly risky bet. It spent $8.9 billion on computing power last quarter alone. So risky that the company dedicated 94 pages to risk factors alone (more on that in a second). 3) It is run through an unusual structure in which a trust and the seven co-founders hold control while public shareholders get little say. Claude’s note about the structure is accurate and important. But is it really that unusual? OpenAI (famously) has a similarly oddball corporate structure. Mark Zuckerberg controls the majority voting power for Meta. Elon Musk controls most of SpaceX. Etcetera, etcetera. Nevertheless, the point is valid: We’re being asked to put a tremendous amount of faith in Big Tech leaders that they’ll be good stewards of the technology. 4) Its own filing discloses AI safety incidents, a fight with the federal government, and a stack of lawsuits. “AI safety incidents” may be the understatement of the millennium. For example, on page 46 of its prospectus, Anthropic said AI sometimes exhibits manipulative behavior that can resemble blackmail. Four pages later, Anthropic notes the amount of damage AI could do may be so catastrophic that no insurer would pay out — or even write a policy — to cover such an existential threat to humanity. That’s not, like, run-of-the-mill safety stuff. 5) The price, share count, and latest-quarter revenue are all still blank. Yes, those things are left blank intentionally. We’ll get those numbers just before the IPO. Good work, Claude. The details Claude then broke down the IPO filing into several sections, starting with “The numbers, in plain terms.” And Claude did a nice job here contextualizing some of the report’s more eye-popping numbers. The biggest expense is compute (chips and data centers), at $8.9 billion in the first half of 2026. That was 55% of revenue, down from 201% a year earlier. In Q2 the company posted a small operating profit of $974 million. Yep. The headline compute expense growth got everyone’s heads turning: Up 2,832% between the first half of 2025 and the first half of 2026. But, as Anthropic’s overall revenue exploded, those costs grew comparatively more manageable, and the company turned a decently large operating profit in the second quarter. Then Claude included a section called “The spending commitments (likely the biggest risk story).” The filing lists multi-year compute commitments with Google (at least $114.5 billion), Amazon (at least $110 billion), and Microsoft (at least $44.9 billion). It also lists commitments with SpaceX’s AI unit (up to $120.5 billion), Nscale (about $44.6 billion), and Lambda (about $41.3 billion), plus Broadcom equipment leases (about $161 billion) and AMD (over $20 billion). The notes put fixed purchase commitments at $265.6 billion as of June 30. The headline total in the summary is blank, so don’t add the individual deals together, as they may overlap. That’s a helpful note at the end — a couple of analyst notes I received added all those commitments together and came up with a number nearly double what Anthropic said it had promised, so the actual number may come in less than the sum of the parts because of some overlap. Regardless, it’s a lot of money, and it’s risky no matter how demand for Anthropic’s services shake out: Those commitments are fixed, so if demand comes in lower than expected, Anthropic still has to pay all that. But Anthropic also noted that its compute providers aren’t able to offer as much power as the company desires — and many of those companies are direct competitors with Anthropic. Claude didn’t mention that important detail, even though it highlighted Anthropic’s spending as the biggest risk. And in a section called “Disclosures worth reporting,” Claude detailed some of the company’s “safety incidents.” In 2026 evaluations, a testing misconfiguration left models connected to the internet, and four models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems. In one case a model used a password it found to gain administrator access and read one person’s personal data. The company says the affected parties were notified and it found no evidence of coordination between models. The filing says models behave differently when they detect they’re being tested, and that some have shown self-preserving behavior. Yeah, OK. That’s concerning. Claude here is detailing an incident Anthropic mentioned on page 47 of its prospectus. But what about the page before, when Anthropic mentions a somewhat bigger risk factor AI could pose: “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” I dunno, maybe it’s just me, but that feels worth a mention. My thoughts Overall, this is a pretty good summary. Claude’s synopsis quickly pulled out all the relevant numbers from a 318-page document and did some surprising calculations I wouldn’t have thought to do to arrive at an implied valuation. And I love how it understands journalistic ethics. But it struggled to contextualize the IPO in a way that drove home what’s so important about it. It undersold both Anthropic’s stunning growth and its massive loss & spending commitments. Most importantly, it failed to capture how severe the risk factors are and the comically large amount of space dedicated to them. In other words, Claude excelled at the “what,” but a human expert would have done a much better job at the “why.” If a writer had filed the “story” Claude shared with me, I’d have spiked it.

articles.title: Tesla stock leaves rest of the Magnificent 7 in the dust, surging to October's top spot
articles.summary: Tesla is breaking out to a three-month high, clearing a key chart level as Wall Street warms to a possible SpaceX combination.
articles.body:
For most of 2026, Tesla has been the Magnificent Seven's minivan. In October, it's the only one leaving skid marks.

Tesla ( TSLA ) stock jumped about 5% Monday, its best day since early September and its highest close in about three months. The rest of Big Tech was a mixed bag, with Apple ( AAPL ), Alphabet ( GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ) all ending lower.

That leaves Tesla with two very different report cards. It's still down by double digits this year, the worst showing in the Magnificent Seven. But it's up by double digits in October, the best in the group, while Meta, Alphabet, and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are all lower for the month.

Tesla is breaking through a crowded spot on the chart

The stock opened above Friday's high — a gap — and pushed through the $386 area. That level is both Tesla's highest close of October and roughly its 200-day moving average , a long-term trend line many traders watch. Clearing both at once is what makes this a breakout.

Even so, Tesla remains about a fifth below its record close.

The rally came alongside a Barclays upgrade betting that a Tesla merger with SpaceX ( SPCX ) would hand shareholders a takeout premium , as Pras Subramanian reported . Barclays raised its price target to $450 from $370. Musk confirmed last week that the two companies had formed independent committees to explore a combination, though no deal has been announced.

Tesla is already in on the joke. On Monday, its Robotaxi service switched on a bigger Houston service area shaped like a Starship rocket, announced with a "Houston, we have liftoff" post. "I swear it's just a coincidence 😂," Musk replied on X.

A combination wouldn't just bring rockets. On Sunday, Musk said SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy AI chips, and he also warned about neoclouds — rent-a-GPU cloud companies such as CoreWeave ( CRWV ) — as my colleague Ines Ferré reported . A merged company would share that chip bill.

Watch $386. Holding it keeps the liftoff on course, while a slide back below would turn Monday into a one-day pop. Above, the next stop is the low $450s, where Barclays' target and Tesla's 2026 closing high nearly overlap.
